claim: Wearing face masks will stop the spread of covid 19
justification: According to major public health organizations such as the [WHO](https://www.vox.com/2020/6/6/21282108/masks-for-covid-19-world-health-organization-guidelines-cloth-n95) and [CDC](https://abcnews.go.com/Health/cdc-offer-conflicting-advice-masks-expert-tells-us/story?id=70958380), face masks are recommended as one layer within a multi-layered prevention strategy, not as a standalone measure to stop COVID-19 transmission. While different mask types offer varying degrees of filtration efficiency—ranging from as low as 2–3% for some cloth masks to over 95% for N95 respirators ([NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7497125/))—no peer-reviewed study or meta-analysis concludes that masks provide 100% protection against inhaling or expelling SARS-CoV-2 particles ([medRxiv](https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.04.01.20049528v1)). The primary mechanism of masks involves source control and partial wearer protection, but practical limitations such as poor fit, incorrect material, inconsistent use, and the inability of even well-fitted medical masks to completely block virus droplets or aerosols ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33087517/)) prevent masks from being an absolute barrier to transmission. Evidence from community randomized trials ([FHI](https://www.fhi.no/en/publ/2020/Should-individuals-in-the-community-without-respiratory-symptoms-wear-facemasks-to-reduce-the-spread-of-COVID-19/)) indicates only a small protective effect, and outbreaks have been documented even in populations with high mask compliance. Public health guidance consistently frames masks as part of a combined strategy alongside vaccination, ventilation, social distancing, and hand hygiene ([American Lung Association](https://www.lung.org/blog/covid-masks)), making the claim that masks alone will "stop" COVID-19 spread unsupported by the scientific evidence.
judge_reasoning:
### Step 1: Summary of Key Insights
The fact-check shows that major public health organizations like the WHO and CDC consistently state that masks alone do not guarantee complete cessation of COVID-19 transmission; they are recommended as one layer within a multi‑layered prevention strategy. Peer‑reviewed studies and meta‑analyses conclude that masks reduce but do not eliminate risk, with no evidence of 100% protection. Masks primarily work through source control and offer some wearer protection, but practical limitations—such as poor fit, incorrect material, inconsistent use, and incomplete filtration even when well‑fitted—prevent them from being an absolute barrier. Documented outbreaks have occurred in populations with high mask compliance, and the emergence of more transmissible variants like Delta led to updated guidance (e.g., universal indoor masking), further indicating that masks cannot single‑handedly stop spread.

### Step 2: Missing Information
The evidence is comprehensive and consistent in showing that masks do not “stop” the spread completely. No authoritative source claims absolute protection, and the recorded limitations and real‑world examples adequately address the claim. Therefore, no further investigation is required.

### Step 3: Conclusion
Based on the recorded evidence, the claim that “Wearing face masks will stop the spread of covid 19” is `refuted`.

This survey reported median white household wealth of $188,200 and median Black household wealth of $24,100, yielding a ratio of approximately **7.8 to 1**, not 81 to 1 ([Federal Reserve 2020](https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/notes/feds-notes/disparities-in-wealth-by-race-and-ethnicity-in-the-2019-survey-of-consumer-finances-20200928.htm)). No credible survey directly states an 81:1 ratio; major sources consistently report single-digit ratios ([Federal Reserve 2020](https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/notes/feds-notes/disparities-in-wealth-by-race-and-ethnicity-in-the-2019-survey-of-consumer-finances-20200928.htm)). A conflict regarding a cited 81:1 ratio trend from another source was resolved in favor of the Federal Reserve data, as it is the definitive primary source.
judge_reasoning:
### Step 1: Key Insights from Fact-Check
The fact-check establishes that the most authoritative source for U.S. median household wealth by race is the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF). According to the 2019 SCF data, the median white household wealth was $188,200 and the median Black household wealth was $24,100, yielding a ratio of approximately 7.8:1—far lower than the claimed 81:1. The retrieved document from the Federal Reserve directly states these figures and explicitly notes the ratio is "about eight to one." A separate document from Prosperity Now mentions an 81:1 ratio in a different context (projecting 2020 figures), but the most recent and definitive SCF data from 2019 does not support that claim. The reasoner in memory, having no recall of an 81:1 ratio from any standard source, aligns with the SCF data.

### Step 2: Missing Information
The evidence is clear and no further investigation is required. The authoritative source (the 2019 SCF) provides specific median wealth figures that directly contradict the claimed ratio. The only source mentioning an 81:1 ratio is not the SCF and uses different methodology or projections, which does not match the claim as stated without a specified timeframe or source.

### Step 3: Conclusion
Based on the recorded evidence, the Federal Reserve's 2019 Survey of Consumer Finances—the most recent and authoritative source—reports a median white-to-Black household wealth ratio of about 7.8:1, not 81:1. The claim is explicitly contradicted by this data. Therefore, the decision is `refuted`.

claim: A law called The Flora and Fauna Act classified aboriginal people as animals until Australian voters overturned it in the 1960s.
justification: Extensive research, including examination of legislative records and historical archives, found no evidence of any Australian law officially titled "The Flora and Fauna Act" or one that explicitly classified Aboriginal Australians as flora or fauna; this is consistently described as a persistent urban myth ([Club Troppo](https://clubtroppo.com.au/2013/06/03/were-indigenous-people-regulated-by-the-flora-fauna-act/), [SBS](https://www.sbs.com.au/nitv/article/shareena-clanton-is-like-many-of-us-a-victim-of-the-flora-and-fauna-act-myth/m40dgtgah)). judge_reasoning:
Based on the recorded fact-check, the evidence overwhelmingly and consistently shows that no Australian law titled "The Flora and Fauna Act" ever existed, and Aboriginal Australians were never legally classified as "flora" or "fauna." The 1967 referendum successfully amended the Constitution to grant the federal government power to legislate for Aboriginal people and include them in population counts; it did not repeal any act by that name. Both independent sources (retrieved documents and memory-only reasoner) agree on these points, with the specific details and conflicts found in the record being peripheral to the central, undisputed facts.

No further information is lacking; the evidence is clear and conclusive.
